title: A command-line sampling tool
description:
### Task
Complete the argument parser and use `random.Random(seed).randint(1, 6)` count times. Print the label and generated integers. A seed makes the result repeatable.

### Input
Command-line arguments `--label` (text), `--seed` (non-negative integer), `--count` (integer 1–10). No stdin.

### Output
`<label>: <numbers joined by spaces>`.

### Assumptions
All inputs satisfy the stated limits. Do not print input prompts.

### Example
Input:
```text
Arguments: --label sample A --seed 7 --count 3
```
Result:
```text
sample A: 3 2 4
```

### Hint
Create the generator once, before the loop. Do not reset its seed for every value.

Difficulty: **harder**.
solution:
import argparse
import random
parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--label", required=True)
parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, required=True)
parser.add_argument("--count", type=int, required=True)
args = parser.parse_args()
rng = random.Random(args.seed)
values = [rng.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(args.count)]
print(args.label + ": " + " ".join(map(str, values)))
starter_code:

title: Organise files and compare copies
description:
### Task
Create `selected` and copy only the input directory's top-level `.txt` files there with `shutil.copyfile()`. Print copied basenames alphabetically. Then compare all copied files using `filecmp.cmp(..., shallow=False)`.

### Input
One supplied directory path.

### Output
Copied basenames, one per line, followed by `copies identical: yes` when every copy matches (also when no files match). Create exactly those copies under `selected`.

### Assumptions
All inputs satisfy the stated limits. Do not print input prompts.

### Example
Input:
```text
python-course/copy-a
```
Result:
```text
A.txt
sample B.txt
copies identical: yes
```

Generated file/content:
```text
selected/A.txt: alpha
selected/sample B.txt: beta
```

### Hint
The supplied imports and directory creation are scaffolding; complete the copy loop.

Difficulty: **medium**.
solution:
import glob
import os
import shutil
import filecmp
directory = input()
os.mkdir("selected")
identical = True
for source in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(directory, "*.txt"))):
    if not os.path.isfile(source):
        continue
    name = os.path.basename(source)
    target = os.path.join("selected", name)
    shutil.copyfile(source, target)
    identical = identical and filecmp.cmp(source, target, shallow=False)
    print(name)
print("copies identical: " + ("yes" if identical else "no"))

title: Summarise a tiny variant table
description:
### Task
Read a simplified TSV. Ignore lines beginning with `#`; the first remaining line is the header `CHROM`, `POS`, `EFFECT`. Keep `stop_gained` and `frameshift` rows and write columns `chrom,position,effect` to `variants.csv` in original order. These labels identify two example kinds of sequence change.

### Input
One supplied TSV filename. Fields are tab-separated; positions are positive integers.

### Output
Create `variants.csv` with the lowercase header, minimal CSV quoting and `
` line endings. Print nothing.

### Assumptions
This documented, simplified table is not a complete VCF format. Inputs are valid. Do not print prompts.

### Example
Input:
```text
python-course/variants-a.tsv
```
Result:
```text
(no console output)
```

Generated file/content:
```text
chrom,position,effect
1,100,stop_gained
2,80,frameshift
```

### Hint
Pass only non-comment lines into `csv.DictReader(..., delimiter="	")`.

Difficulty: **harder**.
solution:
import csv
filename = input()
with open(filename, encoding="utf-8") as source, open("variants.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as target:
    reader = csv.DictReader((line for line in source if not line.startswith("#")), delimiter="	")
    writer = csv.writer(target, lineterminator="\n")
    writer.writerow(["chrom", "position", "effect"])

title: Plot small group counts
description:
### Task
Count rows belonging to groups A and B in the CSV, including zero for an absent group. Save a bar chart as counts.png. Use matplotlib defaults, a 4 × 3 inch figure at 100 DPI, bars A then B, title `Sample counts`, x-label `Sample`, y-label `Count`, and y-limits 0 to max(counts)+1. Call tight_layout before saving; close afterward.

### Input
One CSV filename with sample,group columns; group is A or B. Header-only CSV is allowed.

### Output
Print `Counts: <A>, <B>` and create a 400 × 300 pixel counts.png. The values and chart appearance are graded; small rendering differences are tolerated.

### Assumptions
All inputs satisfy the stated limits. Do not print input prompts.

### Example
Input:
```text
python-course/groups-a.csv
```
Result:
```text
Counts: 2, 3
```

Generated file/content:
```text
counts.png: bars A=2 and B=3, with the specified title and axis labels
```

### Hint
A display window is unnecessary. Keep default colours/width/style and use `plt.figure`, `plt.bar`, `plt.title`, `plt.xlabel`, `plt.ylabel`, `plt.ylim`, `plt.tight_layout` and `plt.savefig`.

Difficulty: **harder**.
solution:
import csv
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
counts = {"A": 0, "B": 0}
with open(input(), newline="", encoding="utf-8") as source:
    for row in csv.DictReader(source):
        counts[row["group"]] += 1
values = [counts["A"], counts["B"]]
print(f"Counts: {values[0]}, {values[1]}")
plt.figure(figsize=(4, 3), dpi=100)
plt.bar(["A", "B"], values)
plt.title("Sample counts")
plt.xlabel("Sample")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.ylim(0, max(values) + 1)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("counts.png")
plt.close()

title: Detect edges in a synthetic image
description:
### Task
Load the grayscale PNG as a floating-point array with values 0–1 using skimage.io.imread(..., as_gray=True) and img_as_float. Run feature.canny with sigma=1.0, low_threshold=0.1 and high_threshold=0.2. Print the number of true pixels, then mask rows 4 and 8 as contiguous 0/1 strings.

### Input
One small grayscale PNG filename. Rows 4 and 8 always exist.

### Output
`edges: <count>`, `row4: <bits>`, `row8: <bits>`. Each bit string has one character per image column.

### Assumptions
All inputs satisfy the stated limits. Do not print input prompts.

### Example
Input:
```text
python-course/square-a.png
```
Result:
```text
edges: 28
row4: 0000111111110000
row8: 0000100000010000
```

### Hint
A true mask pixel marks an edge. The synthetic examples isolate this operation; no circle detector or photograph analysis is required.

Difficulty: **harder**.
solution:
from skimage import io, feature, img_as_float
image = img_as_float(io.imread(input(), as_gray=True))
mask = feature.canny(image, sigma=1.0, low_threshold=0.1, high_threshold=0.2)
print(f"edges: {int(mask.sum())}")
for row in [4, 8]:
    print(f"row{row}: " + "".join("1" if value else "0" for value in mask[row]))
